strengths: First second-order and path-length regret bounds for online tabular MDPs, extending prior first-order results into a richer family of data-dependent measures within a unified best-of-both-worlds framework.

Careful and technically deep adaptation of OFTRL machinery (loss-shifting, dilated bonuses, virtual episodes) to handle refined data-dependent quantities, including new loss/Q-function estimators and variance decompositions tailored to MDP dependency structure.
Novel optimistic Q-function estimator with controlled bias margin (γtH/qt(s)) for policy optimization, a technically elegant contribution of potential independent interest.
Nearly matching lower bounds (L⋆, Q∞, V1, V) via a clean truncation-based construction, substantiating near-optimality claims for the global-optimization approach.
Thorough, quantitative comparison with prior work (Tables 1-3, Appendix B.2), clarifying concrete improvements over Jin et al. 2021 and Dann et al. 2023b.
Proofs appear internally consistent and mostly self-contained across an extensive appendix.
weaknesses: Restriction to known transition dynamics is a major limitation; extension to unknown transitions (arguably the more practically relevant setting) is explicitly left open, especially for policy optimization.
Path-length upper bound (√(SA·V1)) leaves an unresolved √(SA/H) gap relative to the lower bound (√(H·V1)).
Policy-optimization bounds carry an extra multiplicative H factor relative to global optimization, and this gap is not closed.
No empirical validation; all results are purely theoretical, leaving open questions about practical numerical behavior/stability of the adaptive learning rate and estimator schemes.
Very dense presentation with heavy notation overload and most substantive content deferred to a lengthy appendix, making independent verification challenging.

The algorithm cannot simultaneously attain path-length and variance-aware gap-dependent bounds; the predictor (gradient-descent vs. empirical mean) must be chosen a priori, slightly undermining the single-algorithm best-of-both-worlds framing.
Several stochastic-regime bounds include additive lower-order terms with high polynomial dependence on S, A, H whose tightness/practical relevance is unclear.

strengths: Introduces several new, well-motivated complexity measures (second-order Q∞, path-length V1, occupancy-weighted variance V and conditional variance V^c) that extend known bandit-theoretic notions to the tabular MDP setting for the first time.

Provides a unified best-of-both-worlds algorithmic framework (via OFTRL with log-barrier and adaptive learning rates) that simultaneously achieves multiple types of data-dependent and variance-dependent guarantees, covering both global optimization and policy optimization approaches.

Establishes nearly matching information-theoretic lower bounds (Section 6) for L*, Q∞, V1, and V, demonstrating that the global-optimization upper bounds are near-optimal, which substantially strengthens the paper's contribution.

Technical innovations are non-trivial and clearly explained: the invariant-function/loss-shifting construction compatible with OFTRL stability, and a new optimistic Q-function estimator for policy optimization with controlled, quantifiable bias.

The variance measures V and V^c are shown to be sharper (by a factor of H^2) than prior variance notions (Var_max, Var^c_max) used in value-based approaches, and the paper connects this improvement concretely to the resulting regret bounds.

The paper is thorough in tracing implications (e.g., the gap-dependent bound improves over Jin et al. 2021 by removing dependence on 1/min Δ(s,a)) and provides extensive comparison tables against prior work.
Limitations (known-transition restriction, H-gap between policy and global optimization, path-length gap) are explicitly and honestly acknowledged as open problems rather than obscured.
weaknesses: The known-transition assumption is a substantial restriction; the paper explicitly defers the more practically relevant unknown-transition setting to future work, limiting immediate applicability.
No empirical evaluation is provided; while this is standard for regret-bound papers of this type, it leaves open the practical impact of the improved bounds.

Policy optimization results retain an extra factor of H relative to global optimization (and relative to the lower bounds), a longstanding open gap in this line of work that this paper does not close.
The path-length upper bound (Theorem 4.1) has an unresolved √(SA/H) gap relative to the corresponding lower bound (Theorem 6.1), acknowledged but unaddressed by the authors.

Substantial portions of the algorithmic framework (log-barrier OFTRL, loss-shifting technique, dilated bonus construction) are adapted from Jin et al. (2021), Luo et al. (2021), and Dann et al. (2023a), somewhat limiting the conceptual novelty despite meaningful technical extensions.
The manuscript is extremely dense with heavy notation and a large number of lemmas, which may hinder accessibility and independent verification by readers outside the immediate subfield.
